en: The Sutra on Mahākāśyapa’s Journey to the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Tanwulan of the Western Regions during the Eastern Jin Dynasty.
Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, Mahākāśyapa was the eldest among all the bhikṣus.
Tārkṣya was talented, brilliant, and wise; his body also possessed the golden marks and signs of excellence.
Whenever the Buddha preached the Dharma, he would always sit facing him, and when the people saw him, some called him the "Teacher of the Buddha."
Thereupon Kāśyapa took his leave of the Buddha and went to Mount Isigili.

One mountain there was named Punnaka, which circled for several thousand *li* and was located twenty-six thousand *li* from the kingdom of Śrāvastī. It produced much of the seven treasures, its sweet fruits were beyond measure, and it yielded three kinds of famous incense, fine medicines, and sandalwood:
one kind was fragrant, one kind cured a hundred ailments of humans, and one kind could be used to dye the five colors.
There were incalculable varieties of fragrant herbs and medicinal plants.
There were also birds and beasts that ran and flew about—lions, tigers, wolves, white elephants, qilin, vermilion birds, and phoenixes.
There was a certain pure ascetic of a heterodox school.

At that time, there was a square stone, level and even, its color like lapis lazuli, measuring one hundred and twenty li in length and breadth. Exquisite trees provided cool shade, and flowers and leaves of five colors grew luxuriantly upon the stone throughout both winter and summer.

Kāśyapa previously and subsequently instructed two thousand disciples, all of whom were of pure and noble conduct and had attained arhatship; they constantly sat upon this rock to recite the sūtras and practice the Way.
Furthermore, there is pure, sweet-smelling spring water that encircles the area for forty li; within this water grow udumbara flowers—flowers of deep blue, red, and purple.
Seven disciples of Kāśyapa had the same dream on the same night:
one bhikṣu dreamed that the square stone upon which he sat split apart in the center, and all the trees were uprooted;
another bhikṣu dreamed that the spring water for forty li completely dried up and all the flowers withered and fell.
One bhikṣu dreamed that the seats surrounding Kura were all collapsing and ruined;
another bhikṣu dreamed that the land of Jambudvīpa was all sinking and subsiding;
another bhikṣu dreamed that Mount Sumeru collapsed.
One bhikṣu dreamed that the Golden Wheel-Turning King had passed away;
another bhikṣu dreamed that the sun and moon fell to the earth, leaving the world in darkness.
Rising at dawn, they each reported their dreams to Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa said: "Previously we saw a great radiance and the earth shook violently; now you all have had this dream as well—the Buddha is about to enter parinirvāṇa."
He immediately commanded his disciples to go to the kingdom of Kuśinagara.
On the way, they saw a brahmin carrying *mandārava* flowers.
Kāśyapa then asked him:
“From where have you come?
Where do you intend to go?
How did you obtain these celestial flowers?”
He replied, "I have come from the kingdom of Kuśinagara; seven days have already passed since the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa.
The devas went there and all brought celestial flowers and celestial incense to make offerings to the Buddha’s body; these flowers are those very ones."
Upon hearing these words, Kāśyapa threw himself to the ground and, weeping, said:
"Now that the Buddha is entering parinirvāṇa, the Three Realms are left sightless; upon whom shall we rely?"

He then led his disciples forward on the path; before they had traveled even several hundred *li*, they beheld the Four Heavenly Kings and the various devas of the Brahma and Śakra realms, all holding canopies of the seven treasures, famous incenses, and exquisite flowers, coming together to make offerings to the Buddha. The devas performed music of the twelve divisions, while the Asura kings and great spirits and deities filled the air. Furthermore, they saw the King of Kuśinagara and the kings of neighboring states, each accompanied by their retinues numbering in the hundreds of thousands.
Seeing Kāśyapa approaching with his disciples, the noble King Malla of the country then commanded all the people to clear the way, so that Kāśyapa and his disciples might pass through.
Aniruddha went out to meet him, and upon seeing him, said:
"The Buddha has been in parinirvāṇa for seven days; the fire for the cremation will not ignite, waiting only for the arrival of the Venerable One."
When Ānanda saw Kāśyapa, he threw himself to the ground and wept, unable to restrain himself.
An elder bhikṣu named Pāthikaputta then stopped Ānanda, saying:
“Stop, stop! Do not weep!”
"When the Buddha was alive, he constantly restrained us, so that we could not act with freedom.
Now that the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa, we have attained autonomy.
Do not weep any longer."
At that time, a deva who heard Pāṭihāra’s words immediately raised his hand to strike him. Kāśyapa stepped forward to seize him, but the deva stopped him and said to Pāṭihāra:
"The Buddha has now entered parinirvāṇa; everyone has lost their reliance. Yet you alone are so foolish as to feel joy and satisfaction."
When Pāṭikā heard these words, she understood their meaning and immediately attained the path of Arhatship.
Kāśyapa then, together with his disciples, prostrated himself with his head to the ground, circumambulated the coffin three times, and spoke with sorrow:
"Today we do not know where the Buddha’s head and feet are located."
By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he then extended his foot; among the devas and humans, there were none who were not moved with deep emotion.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa spoke a verse in praise of the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha is the vehicle for the three realms, Who ferries beings across the abyss of birth and death.”
Serene and detached, he ascends to Nirvāṇa; subtle and wondrous, he transcends the world.
The Buddha is immeasurable light, illuminating the darkness of ignorance;
may he, for the sake of all people, manifest his majestic spiritual power.
The Buddha, out of great compassion and pity, has delivered beings beyond measure;
his honored body now rests within the golden coffin, pure, tranquil, and at peace.
May you, through your harmonious virtue, allow us to behold the radiance of your physical marks and features.
Universally causing gods and humans to give rise to immeasurable merit;
the Buddha reveals the Dharma for them, and sentient beings receive its nourishment.
They attain cessation of the wheel of birth and death, and some enter into the True Truths.
Having already received the grace of the Tathāgata, I prostrate my head at the Buddha’s feet.
Now beholding only the golden coffin, my heart is moved by sorrow;
though the Buddha has entered the unconditioned, the realization of the Sage is not unreal.
Seeing the Truth that removes doubt, he extended his feet from the golden coffin;
though this manifestation of birth and death has ended, the Buddha no longer grieves.
The Dharma-body and wisdom abide forever; do not say that he has entered eternal Nirvana.
The Sutra on Kāśyapa’s Journey to the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
